question: Will the UK increase the qualifying period for settlement to 10 years before May 2026?
summary: Objections about carve-outs mean the 10-year baseline may not apply universally to all settlement routes by May 2026.
Implementation hinges on late-2025/early-2026 consultation and potential parliamentary steps, raising near-term risk of delay.
Political, legal, and administrative risks could slow rollout or necessitate transitional rules.
Despite momentum in official materials, the ensemble assumed universal application; adjust downward to reflect structural uncertainties.

justification.critique_assessment: The objections are valid and reveal a genuine blind spot in assuming a universal, immediate 10-year baseline by May 2026.
justification.adjustment: Lowered from 0.92 to 0.82; range 0.74–0.90 to reflect near-term implementation risk and policy carve-outs, while maintaining a high overall likelihood due to policy momentum.

forecasts.reference-class: UK immigration settlement policy reform proposals to raise the baseline qualifying period for settlement from 5 to 10 years, with potential reductions based on contributions; active consultation in early 2026 and possible implementation as early as spring 2026.

sources.claim: House of Commons Library briefing notes that the government announced more details of the proposal on 20 November 2025, establishing a baseline 10-year qualifying period for settlement with a consultation running into February 2026.
Law firm summary describing the consultation and the proposal for a 10-year baseline settlement period, with potential reductions for certain categories.
UK Employment Hub notes the standard baseline qualifying period would increase from five to ten years and mentions potential implementation as early as April 2026.
Freeths article explaining the earned settlement proposals to extend the baseline to 10 years, with possible reductions based on criteria.
GOV.UK guidance confirming the long residence route requires 10 years and how time can be counted from various routes, providing context for the baseline reference point.
The government announced more details on 20 November 2025; the baseline qualifying period for many migrants would be ten years, with exceptions based on circumstances.
Earned settlement proposes increasing the standard qualifying period for settlement to ten years, with potential reductions based on contributions to the economy and society.
Analyses indicate the standard waiting period could rise from five to ten years, with important carve-outs and variations by route and circumstances.
Financial Times reports Reform UK and Labour proposals to tighten settlement criteria, including longer residency requirements and potential 10-year baselines.
Guardian coverage notes the earned settlement model could extend routes to settlement (potentially up to 20 years for some) and discusses consultation outcomes and public funding implications.
Long residence already targets a 10-year qualifying period for settlement, with time counted from multiple lawful residence routes and various exemptions.
The May 2025 immigration white paper proposed increasing the standard qualifying period for permanent residence from five to ten years, with implementation planned to begin in April 2026.
GOV.UK states that the default qualifying period for settlement will be increased from 5 to 10 years, with a 'time adjustment' model allowing reductions for contributions.
Electronic Immigration Network reports that the Home Office launched a consultation proposing to double the ILR qualifying period to 10 years, with potential exceptions.
KPMG notes proposed settlement timelines including a 10-year baseline and various longer periods for certain groups under the Earned Settlement framework.
